extracted.intended_audience: seminary students, theologians, clergy, and advanced readers of Catholic dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_short: dogmatic theology on grace and merit
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition of Catholic dogmatic theology treating the nature of grace and the theological notions of merit (condign and congruous), objects of merit (gratia prima/secunda, gloria prima, increase of glory), and related questions (final perseverance, merit for others, temporal blessings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Merit (Council of Trent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tridentine Council names as objects of merit: (1) the second grace (gratia secunda) as an object of strict merit, (2) eternal life (gloria prima), and (3) increase of glory (increase of heavenly glory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses the distinction between gratiaprima (which the Council excludes from strict merit) and other objects of merit. It raises the question whether gloria prima can be merited and examines cases (infants, baptized adults, catechumens) showing different treatments: infants in baptismal grace owe glory to God's mercy (titulus haereditatis), baptized adults already possess a legal title to gloria prima, whereas catechumens or those justified by perfect contrition may merit gloria prima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condign Merit (meritum de condigno) requires state of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Condign merit (strict merit) is a claim grounded on justice and requires the state of sanctifying grace as a requisite for true (condign) meriting of reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condign merit gives a real claim to a reward (de condigno). The text emphasizes that without sanctifying grace no condign merits can be acquired and that mortal sin annihilates the state of grace and former merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruous Merit (meritum de congruo) gives only a quasi-claim and does not require state of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruous merit (meritum de congruo) differs from condign merit: it does not confer a real claim in strict justice but a quasi-claim based on equity (ex quadam aequitate, congruentia, decentia); it does not require the state of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although analogous to condign merit in many respects, congruous merit is distinct in that it lacks the same juridical force. Some scholastics rejected the term due to ambiguity, but the chapter defends its use and notes that requisites are identical to condign merit except for the requirement of state of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect contrition can merit gloria prima (de condigno) prior to sacramental reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Catechumens and Christians justified by an act of perfect contrition before Baptism or Penance merit for themselves de condigno, not the first grace of justification, but the gloria prima, because perfect contrition is an opus operans that, when infused, becomes an opus meritorium entitled to eternal glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an uncontroversial consequence: perfect contrition at the moment of infusion is meritorious (strictly) with respect to eternal glory, even though it does not replace the sacramental medium for justification in other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptized adults' good works increase but do not merit gloria prima (titulus haereditatis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adults who preserve baptismal innocence until death already possess a legal title to gloria prima through Baptism (titulo haereditatis); therefore their good works increase but do not strictly merit gloria prima.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they hold a hereditary title to eternal life by Baptism, further good works augment their glory (increase) rather than produce a new claim to the first glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of heavenly glory is conditioned on additional good works
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of heavenly glory corresponds to an increase of grace, which is conditioned upon the performance of additional good works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural proofs (Matt. 16:27; 1 Cor. 3:8) and the unequal apportionment of glory in Heaven are used to argue that meritorious works performed on earth causally contribute to differing degrees of glory; inequality of grace (augmented by works) explains inequality of glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: A sinner cooperating with actual grace can merit de congruo to obtain dispositions for justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A Christian in the state of mortal sin, from the moment he begins to cooperate with supernatural (actual) grace, can merit de congruo by good works and obtain by prayer the dispositions necessary for justification, and ultimately justification itself (as an equity-based claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching is supported by Scripture and Augustine; prayer is contrasted with condign merit—'Prayer relies on mercy, condign merit on justice.' Conscientious preparation with actual grace probably merits an additional equitable claim to justification. Passages and patristic/supporting authorities are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of supernatural merit include sanctifying and actual grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace is presented as the sole formal cause of justification and as a necessary requisite of condign merit; actual (cooperating) grace is also necessary for meritorious acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly ties meritoriousness to both habitual (sanctifying) grace and actual grace for acts; earlier and cross-referenced sections (e.g., 'As a requisite of supernatural merit, 413 sqq.') list and discuss these requisites in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final perseverance cannot be merited in strict justice but can be merited de congruo
rubrics_metrics.description: The grace of final perseverance (donum perseverantiae) cannot be merited in the strict sense (de condigno); most authors hold it can be merited de congruo (termed meritum de congruo fallibili).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some deny any meriting at all but admit it can be infallibly obtained by fervent and unremitting prayer. The text treats this as a theologically certain conclusion with broad agreement among theologians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty about meriting future conversion in advance; probable opinions exist
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to answer with certainty whether the just man can merit in advance the grace of conversion against a future lapse into mortal sin; St. Thomas tends to deny it, while Scotus, Bonaventure, and Suarez regard the opposite as a pious and probable opinion supported by Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include the idea that mortal sin interrupts the state of grace and annuls former merits, but other authorities argue merits are not wholly lost and may be imputed with proportion to future sins; prayer for conversion is always useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: The just may congruously merit for others, within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The just man may congruously merit for others those things he may merit for himself (e.g., grace of conversion, final perseverance, the first prevenient grace), owing to the friendship established by sanctifying grace between the just man and God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits: such merits cannot obtain favors that would abrogate the divinely established order of salvation (e.g., justification without grace or a child's justification without Baptism). Prayer for others is often more effective; theological authorities and scriptural examples are cited to confirm practice (Communion of Saints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal blessings can be merited only insofar as conducive to eternal salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal favors (good health, comfortable living, success in business) can be merited, but only insofar as they are conducive to eternal salvation; otherwise they would not be graces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Thomas regards temporal favors conducive to salvation as objects of condign merit and those not related to salvation as objects of congruous merit. The author warns against excessive anxiety for earthly goods, advising orientation of desires and actions toward God, and notes that prayer is more effective than works for obtaining temporal and spiritual favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer is typically more effective than good works in obtaining favors
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer (and the reliance on divine mercy) is presented as more effective than good works in obtaining both temporal and spiritual favors, including conversion and perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural and patristic citations are used (e.g., St. James on the prayer of a just man). The text advises persistent prayer and notes that some favors are infallibly obtained by fervent prayer even when not meritable strictly.
